lead.text: Attacker-controlled JSON numbers reach unguarded BigDecimal conversions in JsonNumberImpl, bypassing the bigIntegerScaleLimit defense. The public accessors intValue() (line 262, sink 264), intValueExact() (267, sink 269), longValue() (272, sink 274), longValueExact() (277, sink 279) and doubleValue() (282, sink 284) all call bigDecimalValue().<conv>() with NO scale check, while the immediately following siblings bigIntegerValue() (287) and bigIntegerValueExact() (297) DO guard with `Math.abs(bd.scale()) <= bigIntegerScaleLimit` and otherwise throw UnsupportedOperationException(NUMBER_SCALE_LIMIT_EXCEPTION). The other number defense does not cover this: JsonTokenizer.getBigDecimal only limits the *source character count* (`sourceLen > jsonContext.bigDecimalLengthLimit()`, line 522, DEFAULT_MAX_BIGDECIMAL_LEN=1100), so a 13-character JSON literal such as {"a":1E+2147483647} passes the length check and yields a BigDecimal with scale -2147483647, which then flows unguarded into intValueExact()/longValueExact(). Source: JsonValueBodyReader.readFrom (rest/.../JsonValueBodyReader.java:69-70, reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1) parses an untrusted HTTP entity with Json.createReaderFactory(null) (defaults), and JsonParserImpl:171 builds the number via getJsonNumber(getBigDecimal(), jsonContext.bigIntegerScaleLimit()). This is the same incomplete-fix shape as the original scale-limit hardening: the limit was applied to the BigInteger accessors only. A verifier must confirm the JDK BigDecimal behaviour (intValueExact/longValueExact perform setScale(0)/toBigInteger, materializing a ~2^31-digit unscaled value) to establish the CPU/memory exhaustion.

reason: The lead's premise is factually wrong and it asserts no actual vulnerability. (1) The claimed "unpinnable-version blind spot" does not exist: all four Maven property placeholders are defined in the SAME root pom.xml the scanner parsed -- jakarta.json-api.version=2.1.2 (line 99), jakarta.annotation-api.version=2.1.1 (line 101), jakarta.xml.bind-api.version=4.0.0 (line 102), jakarta.ws.rs-api.version=3.1.0 (line 103) -- and ${project.version}=1.1.3-SNAPSHOT (line 33). The ${...} strings in :Dependency.version are merely an artifact of the scanner not interpolating Maven properties, which every real SCA tool does as a baseline feature. The analyst's own remediation ("resolve the 7 placeholder versions from the parent POM first") is wrong about where they live; no parent traversal is needed. (2) Three of the seven flagged deps are not third-party at all: parsson, jakarta.json and parsson-media are all groupId org.eclipse.parsson, i.e. this repository's own modules (rest/pom.xml:31, bundles/jakarta.json/pom.xml:31, impl/pom.xml:31), so they cannot be vulnerable third-party components. (3) The resolved third-party versions are clean: jakarta.{json,annotation,xml.bind,ws.rs,servlet}-api are API-only spec jars with no runtime logic; junit 4.13.2 is PAST the fix for the only notable JUnit4 CVE (CVE-2020-15250, fixed in 4.13.1) and is test-scope; hamcrest-core 1.3 is test-scope. (4) jaxb-impl 3.0.1, the one dep the analyst called notable, never ships: it is declared only in the `all` profile dependencyManagement under the comment "dependencies used by demo projects only" (pom.xml:451) and consumed solely by demos/twitter/pom.xml:49-53 at runtime scope, while the shipped artifact org.eclipse.parsson:parsson declares only jakarta.json-api plus test-scope junit (impl/pom.xml:97-102); pom.xml:496-499 confirms the release profile deactivates samples. Parsson is a JSON parser that performs no XML parsing, so the XXE/deserialization rationale is category-level speculation ("XML-binding runtimes are a recurring CVE source"), and "3.0.x superseded by 4.x" is version recency, not a defect. (5) The lead explicitly states it is not asserting any CVE, so there is no vulnerable component to confirm, as CWE-1395 would require. exploit_search returned "corpus unavailable: not indexed", so no exploit reference informed this either way.

lead.text: Inconsistent application of the bigIntegerScaleLimit guard across JsonNumberImpl accessors. The scale check `Math.abs(bd.scale()) <= bigIntegerScaleLimit` is applied ONLY in bigIntegerValue() (lines 290-291) and bigIntegerValueExact() (lines 300-301). The sibling accessors on the same class that also materialize the BigDecimal are NOT guarded: isIntegral() calls `bigDecimalValue().scale()` at line 259 and intValueExact() calls `bigDecimalValue().intValueExact()` at line 269, and per the semantic-search body text intValue()/longValue()/longValueExact()/doubleValue() are likewise unguarded. If any of those JDK BigDecimal accessors internally expands a hostile extreme-scale value (e.g. a parsed `1E-2147483647`) the scale cap is bypassed on that path. IMPORTANT CAVEAT for the verifier: whether this is actually exploitable depends on JDK BigDecimal internals (several of these have fast-paths that return 0 without expansion) AND on whether bigDecimalLengthLimit (default 1100) already rejects such a literal at parse time in JsonTokenizer -- I could not resolve either from the graph alone. Treat as a guard-asymmetry observation to confirm, not an established DoS.

reason: The guard asymmetry is real but is documented as intentional, and the only live hazard candidate cannot be settled in this session. (1) CONFIRMED in source: the `Math.abs(bd.scale()) <= bigIntegerScaleLimit` check exists only in bigIntegerValue() (JsonNumberImpl.java:287-295) and bigIntegerValueExact() (297-305); isIntegral/intValue/intValueExact/longValue/longValueExact/doubleValue (257-285) call bigDecimalValue().xxx() with no check. (2) But JsonConfig.java:21-28 explicitly documents the property as applying only to bigIntegerValue()/bigIntegerValueExact(), so the asymmetry is deliberate scope, not an oversight -- it is a defect only if an unguarded accessor actually expands. (3) The analyst's primary claimed location is DISPROVED: line 259 is isIntegral() -> BigDecimal.scale(), a plain field read with no materialization. intValue()/longValue()/doubleValue() likewise have well-known JDK zero fast-paths (fractionOnly(), scale <= -64, scientific-notation toString), and longValueExact()'s `(precision() - scale) > 19` check cheaply rejects the large-negative-scale case. (4) I DID resolve the analyst's parse-time caveat against them: JsonTokenizer.getBigDecimal() (519-531) limits only the number's source character count (default 1100, JsonContext.java:41), so `1E-100000000` (12 chars) parses fine to scale=100000000, JsonParserImpl.java:171 wraps it in JsonBigDecimalNumber which does not override intValueExact/longValueExact, and the graph shows both base-class methods reachable_from_entry=true. So a hostile extreme-positive-scale value does reach the unguarded *Exact accessors. (5) UNRESOLVED: whether JDK BigDecimal.longValueExact() short-circuits fraction-only values before setScale(0, ROUND_UNNECESSARY) -> bigTenToThe(scale) -> BigInteger.TEN.pow(1e8). That is purely JDK-internal; no java runtime, no Bash tool, and no JDK src.zip/BigDecimal.java exist on this machine, so I could neither read nor execute it. Circumstantially, the CVE-2023-4043 reporters audited this exact class and the maintainers still scoped the guard to only the two BigInteger accessors, which argues the rest are safe. Not enough self-gathered evidence to CONFIRM a DoS, and not enough to fully REJECT the intValueExact/longValueExact path. exploit_search was unavailable ("exploit corpus unavailable: not indexed"), so no version grounding was possible for Parsson 1.1.3-SNAPSHOT (pom.xml:33).
